name: Gowé
what: A wild sedge-like plant whose black tubers are dug up by women, dried in the sun and pounded. It is drunk as a herbal decoction and burned as incense.
smell: Woody and earthy, close to vetiver and cypriol, with hay, myrrh and a dried-fruit sweetness (plum, apricot).
how: Ground tubers are burned at home as incense; a new extract made with women harvesters in northern Senegal is being used in fine perfume.
meaning: Described by its producers as 'the smell of Africa'. Harvesting has become an income source for local women since 2021.

access.note: The dried tuber is sold by some Senegalese sellers abroad, but its botanical name and shipping to Canada need checking. No finished gowé perfume is on sale yet.

botany: Sources disagree on the plant: one names it Cyperus articulatus, another Cyperus rotundus (both sedges). Treat the botanical name as unconfirmed.
verify: Botanical name, local-language names, where it's harvested and how it's prepared.

buy.name: Maison Téranga (Canada)
buy.note: From your research; not checked yet. Confirm the plant and intended use with the seller.

perfumes.name: Amouage gowé perfume
perfumes.note: In development for 2027, using an extract made with women harvesters in northern Senegal.

name: Thiouraye (churai)
what: A home-made incense of wood shavings, fragrant herbs and resins blended with sandalwood, musk, oud or amber, then left to mature for months or years.
smell: Warm, smoky and sweet, different in every household.
how: Burned on charcoal to scent the home, clothes and the body, especially for guests, celebrations and intimacy.
meaning: An unwritten recipe passed from mother to daughter, so each blend carries family memory.

access.note: Sold by Senegalese shops and online sellers, mostly outside mainstream perfume stores. Recipes vary by maker.

perfumes.name: No modern perfume found yet
perfumes.note: A gap: a thiouraye-inspired perfume or fabric scent could be made, as long as it credits the tradition.

name: Kyphi
what: One of the oldest recorded perfume recipes: resins, honey, wine and aromatic plants cooked into a paste and burned.
how: Burned in temples at dusk, used in medicine and in preparing the dead.
meaning: Egyptians linked fragrance to the divine; kyphi was a temple offering.

access.note: Modern recreations exist from incense makers, and some perfumes are inspired by it.

perfumes.name: Temple of Horus
perfumes.note: Canadian incense perfume inspired by a formula on the Temple of Horus walls at Edfu; inspired by it, not a copy of it.

name: Frankincense harvesting
what: Resin tapped by hand from Boswellia trees, the same way for thousands of years, and traded across the ancient world.
how: Burned as incense, chewed, and distilled into oil.
meaning: One of the world's oldest scent trades; Oman's Dhofar coast and the Horn of Africa still supply most of it.

access.note: Frankincense resin and oil are easy to buy, including from Canadian suppliers.

perfumes.name: Temple of Horus
perfumes.note: Frankincense-led incense perfume made in Canada.

name: Uunsi welcome smoke
what: A Somali incense blend burned in a clay burner (dabqaad).
how: Guests wave the smoke over themselves on arrival; it also scents clothes and hair.
meaning: Hospitality and cleansing in one gesture.

access.note: Found through Somali shops and online sellers rather than perfume stores.

name: Scented smoke of the Swahili coast
what: Clothes, hair and bedding are perfumed with fragrant smoke before important occasions.
how: A burner is placed under clothing or a basket so the smoke soaks in.
meaning: Marks weddings and other life moments.

access.note: Mostly made at home or bought locally on the coast; hard to find abroad.

name: Dukhan smoke bath and khumra
what: Women sit wrapped in a blanket over a pit of smouldering fragrant acacia wood (dukhan); khumra is a rich bridal perfume oil blend.
smell: Smoky acacia wood, then layered musk, sandalwood and floral oils.
how: Part of bridal preparation and married women's beauty routines.
meaning: A deeply personal Sudanese ritual of beauty and celebration.

access.note: Smoke wood and blends are sold by Sudanese shops and online sellers; the full ritual is learned, not bought.

name: Bakhoor
what: Wood chips soaked in perfume oils, resins and sugar, burned on charcoal in a mabkhara burner.
how: Passed around to scent guests, clothes and rooms; also wafted through hair.
meaning: A central sign of welcome in Gulf homes.

access.note: Widely sold by Gulf perfume brands and Middle Eastern shops, online and in big Canadian cities.

name: Taif rose distillation
what: Mountain roses picked at dawn each spring and distilled into rose water and precious rose oil.
how: Rose water is used in cooking and to cleanse; the oil is worn as perfume.
meaning: A spring harvest festival and a symbol of the region.

access.note: Genuine Taif rose oil is rare and expensive; check the seller and the origin.

name: Rose water festival (golabgiri)
what: Families distil Damask roses into rose water in copper stills during a spring festival.
how: Rose water flavours sweets and is used in rituals and cleansing.
meaning: A centuries-old seasonal celebration.

access.note: Rose water is sold in most grocery stores; Kashan-origin rose water is harder to find.

name: Attar and mitti
what: Flowers are distilled in copper pots into sandalwood oil (the deg-bhapka method); mitti attar captures baked clay from the riverbed.
smell: Mitti smells like the first monsoon rain on dry earth; floral attars are rich and oily.
how: Dabbed on wrists and clothes; alcohol-free.
meaning: Kannauj has made attars for centuries; mitti is the smell of hope for rain.

access.note: Finished attars are easy to order online; a specific traditional distillation such as true mitti is harder to source.

perfumes.name: Mitti-style petrichor
perfumes.note: A gap: rain-on-earth (mitti) is hard to reproduce consistently, so few modern perfumes do it well.

name: Jasmine garlands
what: Fresh jasmine and other white flowers threaded into garlands for hair, shrines and gifts (gajra in India, phuang malai in Thailand, sampaguita in the Philippines).
how: Worn in the hair, hung at shrines, given as welcome.
meaning: Respect, devotion and welcome.

access.note: Fresh jasmine garlands can sometimes be found at South Asian shops, especially around festivals.

name: Yadom herbal inhalers
what: Small sticks and balms of camphor, menthol, borneol and herbs carried everywhere.
how: Sniffed for freshness in heat, travel and crowds.
meaning: An everyday Thai scent ritual and a favourite souvenir.

access.note: Thai herbal inhalers are sold at Asian grocery stores and online.

name: Kōdō, the way of incense
what: A formal art of appreciating rare woods like kyara agarwood, heated gently rather than burned.
how: Guests 'listen' to incense and play guessing games of matching scents.
meaning: One of Japan's three classical arts of refinement.

access.note: Kōdō sets and genuine aloeswood come from specialist Japanese incense houses; real aloeswood needs careful, legal sourcing.

name: Chinese incense culture
what: Scholars burned blended incense while reading, painting and drinking tea, a culture that peaked in the Song dynasty.
how: Burned in small censers in studies and tea rooms.
meaning: Calm, focus and refinement.

access.note: Chinese incense is easy to find; high-grade agarwood and sandalwood incense is specialist.

name: Scent pouches
what: Small embroidered pouches of fragrant herbs and musk worn on clothing in the Joseon era.
how: Hung from hanbok ties or carried; also used to keep away insects.
meaning: Elegance and protection; an ancestor of today's bag-charm perfumes.

access.note: Easy to make with dried herbs and resin; ready-made pouches from Korean craft sellers.

name: Agarwood incense
what: Vietnam's central coast is famous for agarwood, burned as incense at family altars and temples.
how: Burned daily at ancestor altars.
meaning: Honouring ancestors.

access.note: Genuine agarwood is costly, often faked and trade-restricted, so buy only with clear, legal provenance.

name: Copal smoke
what: Tree resin burned since Maya and Aztec times.
how: Burned in ceremonies, healing rituals and on Day of the Dead altars.
meaning: A bridge between people and the sacred.

access.note: Raw copal resin is fairly easy to find; the tree species and origin vary between sellers.

perfumes.name: Copal resin notes
perfumes.note: Appears as a resin note in some niche perfumes; check which species a perfumer used.

name: Orange blossom water
what: Bitter-orange blossoms distilled each spring into fragrant water.
how: Sprinkled on guests' hands, used in pastries and skin care.
meaning: Welcome and celebration.

access.note: Sold in grocery stores and Middle Eastern shops; neroli oil is a standard perfume material.

buy.name: LVNEA (Montreal)
buy.what: Rose absolute (for comparison with Moroccan rose)

name: Hungary Water
what: A 14th-century rosemary-in-alcohol water, often called the first alcohol-based perfume in Europe.
how: Used as a tonic and a fragrance.
meaning: A bridge from medicine to perfume.

access.note: Rosemary oil and hydrosol are easy to buy; perfumers sell modern versions.

name: Eau de Cologne
what: A light citrus-herbal water created in Cologne in 1709 that gave its name to a whole type of fragrance.
how: Splashed on freely for freshness.
meaning: The start of modern fresh perfume.

access.note: Classic colognes are sold everywhere, including the original Cologne brands.

name: Sacred plants of First Nations
what: Many Indigenous nations hold sweetgrass, sage, cedar and tobacco as sacred medicines.
smell: Sweetgrass smells like vanilla and fresh hay.
how: Used in ceremony and prayer by the communities who keep these teachings.
meaning: Sacred, not a fragrance trend; shown here with respect, not as something to copy or sell.

access.note: Sacred to many First Nations. Buy braids only from Indigenous makers, and leave ceremonial use to the communities it belongs to.

name: Dhofar frankincense
what: Resin tapped from Boswellia sacra trees in southern Oman, traded for thousands of years along the incense routes. Grades are sorted by colour and purity; the pale green-white Hojari is the most prized.
smell: Fresh, lemony and piney when warmed, turning deeper, smoky and mineral as it burns.
how: Burned on charcoal in clay burners to scent homes, clothes and guests; also chewed and soaked in water.
meaning: Hospitality and daily life, and a source of the region's ancient wealth. Wild trees are under pressure, so sustainable harvesting matters.

access.note: Easy: frankincense oil from the same species is sold by Canadian suppliers; good resin grades are specialist.

name: Ylang-ylang of the Comoros and Madagascar
what: Star-shaped yellow flowers picked at dawn and steam-distilled in small island stills. The oil is split into grades by how long it's distilled. Much of it is grown for export to perfumers.
smell: Rich, creamy and sweet, between jasmine and banana custard, with a soft spicy edge.
how: Distilled into oil for the global perfume industry; flowers are also used locally in hair and on bedding.
meaning: A key island livelihood. Being a big export doesn't mean every community has the same traditional uses, so local practice and export crop are kept apart here.

access.note: Easy: ylang-ylang oil is sold by Canadian suppliers. Specific grades and island origins are harder.

name: Haitian vetiver
what: Grass roots dug up by farming families, washed, dried and steam-distilled into one of the most used oils in fine perfume. Haiti is one of the world's main sources.
smell: Earthy, rooty and woody, with a cool green freshness and a hint of smoke and grapefruit.
how: Mostly distilled for export to perfumers; the roots also hold soil on hillsides.
meaning: An important income for thousands of small farmers. A local crop that became a global perfume staple.

access.note: Easy to moderate: Haitian vetiver oil is sold by Canadian perfume suppliers, and many perfumes feature it.

perfumes.name: Le Labo Vetiver 46
perfumes.note: A designer-niche perfume built around Haitian vetiver with pepper, labdanum and incense; sold in Canada.
